stages.title: Market structures: contestability
stages.sub: How firms behave when entry is easy, and why some markets stay as one firm however low costs go.

steps.q: A water company must lay pipes to every house before selling a single litre. As it sells more litres from the same pipe network, what happens to its average cost per litre?
steps.hint: The huge fixed cost of the pipes gets spread over more and more litres.
steps.pre: So average cost falls as output rises. That falling curve is the

steps.q: If that average cost keeps falling right up to the point where one firm is supplying the whole market, could a second firm entering and splitting demand in half produce more cheaply per unit?
steps.right: No, it would have higher average costs
steps.wrong: Yes, it would produce more cheaply
steps.hint: If costs are lowest at the highest output, what happens when output is split between two firms instead of one?

steps.q: A firm can lease a van, deliver in a town for a month, then sell the van and leave with almost all its money back if profits disappear. How risky is entering this market compared to one needing a custom-built factory?
steps.hint: Think about how much money the firm cannot get back if it leaves.
steps.pre: Because sunk costs are so low, firms can dash in and out. That quick in-and-out entry is called

steps.q: In that same town, is it easy for a new delivery firm to start up and just as easy to stop and leave if it does not work out?
steps.right: Yes, both entry and exit are easy
steps.wrong: No, entry is easy but leaving is hard
steps.hint: Low sunk costs mean a firm can walk away with its capital largely intact.

steps.q: An established delivery firm in that town knows any rival could dash in whenever profits look tempting. If it wants to stop rivals bothering to enter at all, should it keep its price high or push it down towards cost?
steps.wrong: Keep it high to maximise profit now
steps.hint: A price that leaves juicy profits is exactly what invites hit-and-run entry.

steps.q: Even though only one firm currently serves the contestable delivery market, it prices near cost purely because rivals could dash in. Does the market behave competitively even with just one firm in it?
steps.right: Yes, the threat of entry alone forces competitive behaviour
steps.wrong: No, only the actual number of firms controls behaviour
steps.hint: Think about what is disciplining the firm's pricing: the firms present, or the firms that could appear.
